name: Social democracy
summary: Social democracy is the family of socialist movements that pursue their aims by peaceful, parliamentary means within liberal democracy, split from communism over Bolshevik dictatorship, and came to seek a socially controlled, mixed market economy with a universal welfare state, strong unions and worker participation. Its own self-definition adds international solidarity, disarmament, development aid and equality between the sexes. The defining sources say little on most cultural, justice and constitutional questions.
scope: Family entry, answered only from sources that define the family as such: the Socialist International's Declaration of Principles (Stockholm 1989), the family's own international self-definition, which speaks of democratic socialism and names socialist, social democratic and labour parties as sharing its values; Michael Newman, Socialism: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford UP, 2005), the scholarly core (maintainer-supplied); and Kathleen Sears, Socialism 101 (Adams Media, 2019), a popular book used at medium confidence at most. Newman's Swedish case study, the SPD, Labour and other member parties' programmes and positions, expert surveys scoring parties, and Bernstein's own writings are not used, because members never answer for the family. Democratic socialism, Third Way, Nordic model and Eurocommunism have their own entries. Berman, Moschonas, Sassoon and Meyer were not available in full text and Britannica returned 403, so they are not cited. The Frankfurt Declaration (1951) could not be opened.

furtherReading.note: A short scholarly account of social democracy and its split from communism.

sources.title: Declaration of Principles, adopted by the XVIII Congress of the Socialist International, Stockholm, June 1989
sources.author: Socialist International
sources.usedFor: The family's own self-definition: democracy, rights, economy, peace, development, gender, technology and environment (paragraph numbers cited).

sources.title: Socialism: A Very Short Introduction
sources.author: Michael Newman, Oxford University Press, 2005
sources.usedFor: Scholarly account of what social democracy is: the break with communism, constitutional route, mixed economy, welfare and unions (maintainer-supplied full text).

sources.title: Socialism 101
sources.author: Kathleen Sears, Adams Media (Simon & Schuster), 2019
sources.usedFor: Popular definition of social democracy as a peaceful, evolutionary route through the existing political process (maintainer-supplied full text; medium at most).

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The Declaration seeks the lowest possible level of defensive weapon systems rather than none (para 30).

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Declaration demands equality of rights and says no person or class may become another's servant (paras 13-14).

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: The Declaration endorses a mixed economy and claims the right to full and adequately rewarded employment and wage earners' influence at work (paras 57, 60, 63), which presupposes wage labour.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The Declaration wants new technology introduced only as social needs and democratic debate decide, and wants socially unacceptable technologies prevented (paras 50, 52).

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: The Declaration condemns proxy struggles by major powers and asks suspension of arms supplies to parties in conflict (paras 32, 34).

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Newman (ch. 1) says social democracy rejected the Leninist route of small-group insurrection and seeking socialism by revolution.

arms-reduction.rationale: The Declaration makes disarmament imperative and seeks the lowest possible level of defensive weapon systems (paras 29-30).

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The Declaration wants equal rights and opportunities for different cultures within each society and calls cultural uniformity a threat to freedom (paras 27, 66).

automate-paid-work.rationale: The Declaration says technology should liberate people from routine work rather than impose unwanted idleness and backs shorter working hours (paras 4, 82).

ban-cartels.rationale: The Declaration wants concentrated private economic power replaced and open, accountable competition fostered at home and abroad (para 63).

bound-labor.rationale: The Declaration says no person, class, sex, religion or race may become the servant of another (para 13).

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The Declaration's pluralism includes free choice among parties and rights for organised minority opinion (paras 19, 21).

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The Declaration lists free expression of opinion among rights socialists protect and calls for cultural democracy (paras 26-27).

central-planning.rationale: The Declaration backs decentralised market mechanisms (para 76) and says markets must function (para 62); Newman (ch. 1) says social democrats rejected the Soviet model.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Declaration frames social security and welfare for all as rights guaranteed by society (paras 26, 57-58), not charity.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Declaration counts decolonisation as progress, criticises colonialism and holds that every nation has a right to self-government (paras 6, 8, 32).

clerical-rule.rationale: Rule by senior religious scholars cannot meet the Declaration's definition of democracy (para 19), and it condemns religious fundamentalism (para 74).

collective-bargaining.rationale: The Declaration lists the right to form unions and strike and union involvement in national economic policy (paras 57, 60), and Newman (ch. 4) notes unions' strengthened bargaining role.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Declaration criticises colonialism and counts decolonisation as progress (paras 6, 8).

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Declaration says democracy requires free choice among alternatives and change of government by the free will of the people (para 19).

cooperative-communities.rationale: The Declaration keeps a mixed economy with markets and public and private enterprise, not property held in common by small communities (paras 59-62).

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The Declaration makes guaranteed individual and minority rights and an independent judiciary part of democracy (para 19).

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The Declaration asks equal rights and opportunities for different cultures within each society and holds that diversity enriches (paras 27, 66).

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The Declaration (para 58) rejects treating economic rights as benefits for passive individuals and calls for social welfare for all, and para 8 counts the growth of the welfare state as real progress.

decide-locally.rationale: Newman (ch. 4, 'lessons') says social democrats have tended toward centralisation at state level, while the Declaration (paras 46, 60) asks for decentralised, participative production and supply structures.

defeat-communism.rationale: The Declaration wants the norm to be that different systems trade, negotiate and cooperate, and supports detente (paras 36, 77).

delink-world-market.rationale: The Declaration wants the South more integrated into the world economy and calls for fairer terms of trade, not for breaking ties (paras 41, 80, 88-89).

democracy-best.rationale: The Declaration calls political democracy an indispensable element of socialism and the precondition for other rights (paras 2, 19-20), and says social policy cannot disguise a dictatorship.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The Declaration adds minority rights, an independent judiciary and economic and social democratisation to free elections (paras 19, 25).

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: The Declaration says democracy requires a free choice between political alternatives and calls it pluralist by its nature (paras 19, 21).

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Newman (ch. 1, 'The break between communism and social democracy') says the Bolshevik party-state dictatorship caused the split, and the Declaration (paras 22, 75) condemns dictatorial government and Stalinism.

direct-action.rationale: Sears (section on syndicalism) says syndicalists rejected social democracy's working within the political system in favour of direct action, and Newman (ch. 1) describes the family's pursuit of change through parties and constitutional means.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Declaration demands equal rights for men and women in practice, at work and in the family (para 17) and full legal equality (para 72).

distribution-by-process.rationale: The Declaration makes basic economic equality and compensation for social inequalities part of justice (para 14), not only the origin of holdings.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The Declaration says cultural diversity enriches rather than endangers societies and urges tolerance among groups (para 66).

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Declaration says the people should exercise control by democracy (paras 2, 56).

duties-before-rights.rationale: The Declaration says individual rights are fundamental to socialist values (para 20) and that rights must be guaranteed to individuals and minorities (paras 19, 26).

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The Declaration says an open world economy can stimulate development and calls for cutting trade barriers (paras 83, 89), not a closed bloc.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Declaration makes free elections and peaceful change of government essential to democracy (para 19).

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The Declaration calls the rights to life, belief, expression, association and protection from torture inalienable (para 26).

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The Declaration calls strengthening the UN an important step toward a democratic world society (para 98) and wants multilateral institutions with a bigger role for the South under UN aegis (para 39).

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Declaration grounds equality in the equal value of all human beings and demands equal rights before an impartial rule of law (paras 14, 19).

equal-outcomes.rationale: The Declaration (para 14) calls basic economic, social and cultural equality essential and demands compensation for physical, mental and social inequalities, beyond equal opportunity.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Declaration calls cultural diversity an enrichment, praises multicultural societies and warns that cultural uniformity threatens freedom (para 66).

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: The Declaration says social and economic democracy are not luxuries only rich countries can afford but necessary for any country to progress, and that cultures will develop their own forms of democracy (paras 21, 90).

existential-risk-priority.rationale: The Declaration says human survival depends on joint action and that nuclear war could end human life (paras 1, 28).

exit-over-voice.rationale: The Declaration calls political democracy the necessary framework for other rights and the prime means of popular control (paras 2, 56), ranking voting above exit.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The Declaration protects the inalienable right to life and protection from torture, and requires the rule of law impartially applied (paras 19, 26).

filial-duty.rationale: The Declaration says elderly people need the respect and support of the young (para 67).

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The Declaration says there is no single or fixed model for economic democracy and room for bold experimentation in different countries (para 61).

free-trade.rationale: The Declaration wants rich countries to open markets and cut trade barriers for the South (paras 80, 83) but warns that an open world economy brings vulnerability (para 89).

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The Declaration (paras 13, 22) demands freedom from arbitrary and dictatorial government and from servitude to others, though it does not frame it as non-domination.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Declaration says justice means the end of all discrimination against individuals (para 14).

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The Declaration backs positive steps ensuring women's representation at all levels of decision making (para 72), without prescribing a legal quota.

gradual-change.rationale: Sears ('What is Social Democracy?') defines it by a peaceful, evolutionary transition through the existing political process, and Newman (ch. 1, 2) says social democrats accepted liberal-democratic institutions as the route to change.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The Declaration makes individual rights fundamental and asks compensation, not prevention, for physical and mental inequalities (paras 14, 20).

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The Declaration says peace cannot be guaranteed by nuclear deterrence and makes disarmament imperative (paras 29, 54).

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The Declaration says the elderly need a guaranteed income through social security and public pension (para 67).

individual-rights-only.rationale: The Declaration speaks of equal rights for races, ethnic groups, nations and denominations and of rights for organised minority opinion (paras 18, 21), not of individuals alone.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The Declaration (paras 4, 51) says technology can serve humankind and that social progress requires technological progress, and Newman (ch. 3) notes social democracy's commitment to industrial growth.

informal-organisation.rationale: Newman (ch. 3) says social democracy assumed socialism is pursued through a party, and Sears says syndicalists' rejection of permanent political organisation set them against it.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: The Declaration builds the new order on respect for national sovereignty and criticises major powers' proxy conflicts (paras 32, 34).

job-guarantee.rationale: The Declaration affirms a right to full and useful employment and says governments must take overall responsibility for full employment (paras 57, 81).

limit-growth.rationale: The Declaration (paras 48, 78) favours qualitative, ecologically balanced growth rather than limiting it, and Newman (ch. 3) records social democracy's priority on industrial growth.

means-match-ends.rationale: The Declaration (para 25) says democracy and human rights are not only means to socialist ends but the very substance of those ends, and para 19 calls democratic socialism a continuing process of democratisation.

military-superiority.rationale: The Declaration says peace cannot rest on deterrence or an arms race (para 29) and seeks the lowest possible level of defensive arms (para 30), which a drive for superiority contradicts.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Newman (ch. 4) says social democrats long assumed public services are publicly provided but that Third Way social democracy moved toward service delivery by mixed providers, so the family has moved.

nation-first.rationale: The Declaration says socialist goals cannot be attained in a few countries alone (para 92) and refuses to let nations shape the world order by their own self-interest (para 97).

national-mission.rationale: The Declaration says different cultures will develop their own forms of democracy and respects national sovereignty (paras 21, 32).

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Declaration gives the state wide duties: regulating markets, social security and welfare for all, full-employment responsibility (paras 57, 64, 81).

one-party-rule.rationale: The Declaration requires a free choice among political alternatives and calls democracy pluralist by nature (paras 19, 21); Newman (ch. 1) records the break with Bolshevik one-party dictatorship.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: Sears gives as the basic tenet of social democracy that socialist reforms can be achieved democratically through the election of socialist representatives; Newman says the family held transformation by peaceful parliamentary means possible.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The Declaration wants substantial involvement of workers and communities in economic decisions and more scope for popular decision-making in working life (paras 51, 61, 63).

party-controls-media.rationale: The Declaration protects free expression and pluralism and sees political openness as part of a progressive society (paras 21, 26, 76).

party-own-road.rationale: The Declaration says the SI is an association of independent parties, not a centralised body, and that each party chooses its own way (paras 93-94).

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Declaration calls inequality between men and women the most pervasive form of oppression in history, persisting in almost every socio-economic order (para 68).

person-over-state.rationale: The Declaration says each individual should live a meaningful life with full development of personality, and individual rights are fundamental (paras 12, 20).

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority resting on personal oaths of loyalty cannot meet the Declaration's test of democracy: free elections and peaceful change of government (para 19).

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: The Declaration says violent ways of handling conflicts destroy opportunities for development and human rights (para 33) and makes peaceful change of government the test of democracy (para 19); Sears says the family seeks a peaceful transition.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The Declaration attributes poverty to institutions: gaps in international political structures and fundamental inequality (paras 7, 99).

population-transfer.rationale: The Declaration requires guaranteed minority rights and equal rights for ethnic groups (paras 18-19), which forced removal would violate.

positive-liberty.rationale: The Declaration (paras 13-14) says freedom means the greatest chance to act on one's goals, requires freedom from dependence on owners of the means of production, and needs basic economic equality.

price-stability-first.rationale: The Declaration calls it of paramount importance that governments take overall responsibility for full employment (para 81) and criticises conservative deflationary policies (para 40), so stable prices are not first.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: The Declaration supports transforming communist societies through liberalisation and democratisation and wants to strengthen democratic socialism in the South (paras 76, 90), with democracy defined by free elections, minority rights and an independent judiciary (para 19).

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Declaration requires the rule of law applied impartially by an independent judiciary and freedom from arbitrary government (paras 19, 22).

property-franchise.rationale: The Declaration requires equal rights and free elections for democracy (paras 14, 19), which a property qualification would defeat.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Declaration (paras 60, 63) endorses socialisation and public property and wants concentrated private economic power replaced, which a very hard-to-override property right would block.

public-ownership.rationale: The Declaration (paras 59-60) keeps socialisation and public property within a mixed economy and public enterprises where necessary, yet says nationalisation is no sovereign remedy; Newman (ch. 2) describes the tradition as working within a primarily capitalist system.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Declaration demands equal rights for all races and free elections (paras 14, 18-19).

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The Declaration seeks equal rights for all races, the end of all discrimination, and calls apartheid a crime (paras 14, 18, 42).

recognize-territorial-claims-from-conque.rationale: The Declaration asks for respect for national sovereignty and the right to national self-government and peaceful, negotiated settlement of conflict (para 32).

regulate-corporations.rationale: The Declaration says the state must regulate the market in the people's interest (para 64) and calls for international monitoring of transnational corporations (para 60).

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: The Declaration says democratic socialists strive for equal rights for all races, ethnic groups, nations and denominations (para 18), which expelling a people from its lands contradicts.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: The Declaration says democratic socialists strive for equal rights for all races, ethnic groups, nations and denominations (para 18), which removing an ethnic group contradicts.

restore-past-order.rationale: The Declaration frames socialism as social progress and a continuing process that each generation sets its own goals for (paras 19, 24, 59), not restoration.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The Declaration says dictatorship is an enemy of genuine development and that democracy is necessary for every country's progress (para 90).

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The Declaration lists the right to strike as a human right (para 57).

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The Declaration calls for a genuinely new international economic order and democratisation of the world financial and economic institutions (paras 60, 79).

return-to-foraging.rationale: The Declaration says the technological revolution can provide the basis of a better world and that social progress requires technological progress (paras 4, 51).

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Sears says social democrats took the name to set themselves apart from socialists who advocated violent revolution and seek a peaceful, evolutionary transition; Newman describes the family as pursuing power through parliamentary means.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The Declaration says traditional development aid remains vital and the UN 0.7% of GNP target must be reached without delay (paras 84-85).

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The Declaration lists passing on the spiritual and cultural heritage among education's goals and asks equal access to the national and global cultural heritage (paras 27, 65).

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The Declaration says development assistance remains vital and aid must be increased (paras 84-86).

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Declaration requires equal rights for men and women in the family (para 17).

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Sears describes social democracy as a peaceful, evolutionary route through the existing political process; the Declaration says society can be "changed, reformed or further developed" (para 24).

smash-state-machine.rationale: Sears defines social democracy as using the existing political process, and Newman (ch. 2) says its parties accept liberal-democratic institutions as the route to change.

social-market-economy.rationale: The Declaration wants markets that function and are regulated, with competition kept open and social goals secured (paras 62-64, 78).

socialism-needs-revolutionary-war.rationale: Sears gives as the basic tenet of social democracy that socialist reforms can be achieved democratically through elected representatives; the Declaration holds the same goals are pursued by peaceful means (paras 12, 19).

socialized-markets.rationale: The Declaration accepts markets within a mixed economy and says neither private nor state ownership alone guarantees efficiency or justice (paras 59-62), so it does not limit markets to publicly or worker-owned firms.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: The Declaration says the priority must be to write down, write off or capitalise poor countries' debts (para 80).

state-class-instrument.rationale: Newman (ch. 1-2) shows social democrats pursuing change through the existing state and parliament, which treats the state as usable rather than a pure class tool.

state-harmful.rationale: The Declaration (para 64) says the state must regulate the market and (para 8) counts the welfare state as progress; Newman (ch. 4) notes social democrats tended toward state-level centralisation.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Declaration requires a possibility of peaceful change of government and full rights for organised minority opinion (paras 19, 21).

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The Declaration says welfare is not a matter of subsidising those on the fringe but of an integrated society with social welfare for all (para 58).

taxation-theft.rationale: Newman (ch. 3) describes social democracy's generous welfare as financed from taxation, which the family embraces.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The Declaration (paras 5, 50) treats technology as shaped by interests, a source of new threats, and in need of social control, not as a cure-all.

technology-design-reflects-political-int.rationale: The Declaration says technology is always guided by particular interests and designed according to human values, whether implicit or explicit (para 50).

torture-always-illegal.rationale: The Declaration lists protection from torture and degradation among the inalienable rights socialists protect (para 26).

total-state.rationale: The Declaration's insistence on pluralism, individual rights and freedom from dictatorial government (paras 19-22) rules out a state directing every area of life.

unions-good.rationale: The Declaration lists the right to form unions and to strike as a human right (para 57) and calls for union involvement in national economic policy (para 60); Newman (ch. 4) ties social democracy's post-war strength to unions' bargaining role.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The Declaration requires change of government by peaceful means and condemns religious fundamentalism (paras 19, 74).

vanguard-party.rationale: Newman (ch. 1) says the centrally controlled vanguard party model was distasteful to socialists who believed in reform and democracy and was the basis of the break with social democracy.

war-builds-character.rationale: The Declaration says war destroys human life and the basis for social development (para 28).

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Declaration says concentrated economic power in few private hands must be replaced and that freedom needs independence from the owners of the means of production (paras 14, 63).

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The Declaration calls for the active participation of all citizens in a project for society (para 58).

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Declaration requires equal rights for men and women in all areas of social life (para 17).

women-suffrage.rationale: The Declaration backs full and equal participation of women in political activity (paras 17, 72).

workers-councils.rationale: The Declaration makes free elections and peaceful change of government the test of democracy (para 19), and Newman (ch. 2) says social democrats accepted liberal-democratic institutions as the main route.

workers-nation.rationale: The Declaration makes solidarity global and says socialist parties must work together internationally (paras 15, 92).

workers-own-party.rationale: Newman (ch. 1) describes social democracy as parties built to serve the working class, and the Declaration speaks of socialist, social democratic and labour parties (para 10).

workers-parties-campaign-reforms.rationale: Newman says the parties of the Labour and Socialist International concentrated on parliamentary means and practical reforms, and Sears describes the family as winning reforms by working within the system.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The Declaration calls for worker participation and joint decision-making at company level (para 60) and for wage earners' influence in their workplace (para 63).

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: The Declaration says the debt crisis produced a net financial flow from developing to industrialised countries and that international structures contribute to poverty (paras 7, 85).

missingStatements.text: Governments should take overall responsibility for achieving full employment.
missingStatements.rationale: The Declaration says governments must in practice take overall responsibility to provide for full employment (para 81).

missingStatements.text: New technologies should be introduced only under democratic social control, after public assessment of their risks.
missingStatements.rationale: The Declaration says technology must be brought under social control and assessed, with innovation introduced as democratic debate decides (paras 50, 52).

missingStatements.text: Democracy and human rights are not only means to socialist goals but the substance of those goals.
missingStatements.rationale: The Declaration says democracy and human rights are the very substance of socialist ends (para 25).

notes: Only a few dozen statements are settled by the defining sources: the Socialist International's Declaration covers democracy, economy, peace, development, gender and technology but is silent on healthcare, taxes, migration, religion-state questions and many others; Newman and Sears define the family mostly by its method (peaceful, constitutional) and its break with Bolshevism. Silence is null. Statements where the Declaration's general values (equal rights, freedom of belief) might bear on specific laws (apostasy, blasphemy, conversion) were left null. Pass of 2026-11-23: answered the 121 statements added since; saved the Declaration (get.js) and the maintainer's Newman and Sears texts in the source library. Themes searched in Newman and Sears for the new statements: method (parliament, revolution, violence, reform), wage labour, abolition. Silence stays null.
